target.title: Reconstructing Speech from Human Auditory Cortex
target.version: Published journal article (the first page does not label a version)

read.pdf: Figures 1–8 and Supporting Figures S1–S7 captions; no tables in text.txt

entries.text: The authors report accurate linear reconstruction of slow and intermediate speech fluctuations, including syllable-rate features.
entries.condition: Human nonprimary auditory cortex/STG population responses; auditory-spectrogram representation.

entries.text: The authors claim that fast temporal features, including syllable onsets and offsets, require a nonlinear temporal-modulation-energy representation.
entries.condition: Comparison is between linear spectrogram and nonlinear modulation representations of speech responses in human STG.

entries.text: The authors claim that best reconstruction accuracy overlaps the spectro-temporal modulation range important for speech intelligibility.
entries.condition: Speech modulation features; the intelligibility range is supported by cited psychoacoustic work, not a listener test in this study.
entries.quote: Reconstruction accuracy was highest within the range of spectro-temporal fluctuations that have been found to be critical for speech intelligibility.

entries.text: The authors claim that decoded representations support readout and identification of individual words from brain activity on single-trial sound presentations.
entries.condition: Word identification was performed on isolated-word reconstructions; the recognition procedure and candidate-set conditions are recorded in t32–t35.

entries.text: The cohort comprised 15 neurosurgical patients with epilepsy or brain tumors; participants had normal language capacity by neurological examination.
entries.condition: Subdural ECoG recordings during neurosurgical care; all participants had normal language capacity as determined by neurological exam.
entries.loc: Materials and Methods, Participants and Neural Recordings

entries.text: Electrode grids were 4 mm center-to-center in 4 participants and 10 mm in 11 participants.
entries.condition: Subdural grids placed according to clinical criteria over left or right fronto-temporal regions.
entries.quote: Electrode grids had center-to-center distance of either 4 mm (N = 4 participants) [46] or 10 mm (N = 11) [24,25].
entries.loc: Materials and Methods, Participants and Neural Recordings

entries.text: ECoG sampling rates were 1,000 Hz in 6 participants, 2,003 Hz in 5, and 3,052 Hz in 4.
entries.condition: Digitally recorded multichannel ECoG before common-average re-referencing and feature extraction.
entries.quote: sampling rate = 1,000 Hz (N = 6 participants) [24], 2,003 Hz (N = 5) [25], or 3,052 Hz (N = 4) [46].
entries.loc: Materials and Methods, Participants and Neural Recordings

entries.text: Signals were common-average re-referenced after artifact/noise-channel removal; Hilbert-Huang high-gamma power was z-scored and used for analyses.
entries.condition: Exception: Figure 4B used 30 bands of 10 Hz from 1–300 Hz; Results/Figure 4 label the high-gamma comparison 70–170 Hz (see t25).
entries.loc: Materials and Methods, Participants and Neural Recordings

entries.text: The participants performed passive listening (5), target-word detection (5), or word/sentence repetition (5).
entries.condition: Task assignment across the 15-patient ECoG cohort.
entries.quote: Tasks included passive listening (N = 5 participants), target word detection (N = 5), and word/sentence repetition (N = 5).
entries.loc: Materials and Methods, Participants and Neural Recordings

entries.text: Isolated words from one native-English female speaker were used with 10 participants; TIMIT sentences from varied male and female speakers were used with 5.
entries.value: 10 participants (words); 5 participants (sentences); words 0.3–1 s; sentences 2–4 s; 16 kHz
entries.condition: Words included nouns, verbs, proper names, and pseudowords; stimuli were played at approximately 70–80 dB through loudspeakers or ear inserts.
entries.quote: Speech stimuli consisted of isolated words from a single speaker (N = 10 participants) or sentences from a variety of male and female speakers (N = 5).

entries.text: The linear spectrogram used a 128-channel auditory filter bank spanning 180–7,000 Hz and was downsampled to 32 frequency channels.
entries.condition: Log-spaced auditory filters with bandwidth approximately 1/12 octave; spectrogram derived from the presented speech waveform.

entries.text: The nonlinear modulation features covered 0.5–8 cycles/octave and 1–32 Hz; the reduced rate-scale form had 60 channels (full representation: 1,920 channels).
entries.condition: Magnitude of a 2-D complex wavelet transform; reduced rate-scale representation used for reconstruction unless stated otherwise.

entries.text: The decoder maps multichannel neural responses to stimulus features with regularized linear regression; the tested feature spaces were spectrogram and nonlinear modulation energy.
entries.condition: Each stimulus channel is reconstructed independently using an electrode-by-time-lag filter; 100 lags at 10 ms in the reconstruction model.
entries.loc: Results; Materials and Methods, Stimulus Reconstruction

entries.text: The authors state that a fitted model can predict arbitrary sounds, including novel speech not used in training.
entries.condition: The study reports offline cross-validated reconstructions; it does not report a separate held-out-speaker test (see t47).

entries.text: Training examples paired stimulus representations with neural responses; each dataset supplied 2.5–17.5 minutes of stimulus-response data for fitting.
entries.unit: minutes of training data, varying by participant
entries.condition: Stimulus and neural data were synchronized and downsampled; paired data were used to fit the reconstruction filters.

entries.text: Model fitting used coordinate gradient descent with early stopping; each dataset was split 80% train, 10% validation, 10% test, with stopping after 50 non-improving iterations.
entries.condition: Validation-set prediction accuracy controlled early stopping; test set was described as independent.
entries.quote: Each data set was divided into training (80%), validation (10%), and test sets (10%).

entries.text: Repeated random subsampling partitioned trials without train/test overlap within a resample; reconstruction used 10 spectrogram resamples and 3 modulation resamples, with test duration 0.8–17.5 minutes across participants.
entries.unit: trial proportions; resamples; minutes of concatenated test data
entries.condition: Identical partitions were used to compare spectrogram and modulation models; the forward encoding models used 20 resamples.
entries.quote: The forward encoding models were estimated using 20 resamples; the spectrogram and modulation reconstruction models were estimated using 10 and 3 resamples, respectively (due to increasing computational load).

entries.text: Before model fitting, stimuli and neural responses were synchronized, downsampled to 100 Hz, and standardized to zero mean and unit standard deviation.
entries.unit: Hz; standardized mean; standardized standard deviation
entries.condition: The text does not specify whether standardization parameters were estimated on training data only (see t48).

entries.text: Informative recording sites were concentrated in posterior STG; the reported MNI distribution center is rendered in the text as x=270, y=229, z=12, Brodmann area 42.
entries.condition: Informative weights were defined by t ratio >2.5 with p<0.05 FDR correction; coordinate signs appear absent in the text extraction and are not reconstructed here.

entries.text: Group mean single-trial reconstruction accuracy was r=0.28, significant against zero across all 15 participants and stimulus sets (one-sample t test, df=14, p<10^-5).
entries.unit: Pearson r; p value; degrees of freedom
entries.condition: Mean over participants and stimulus sets, including different isolated-word sets and continuous sentences from different speakers; spectrogram model.
entries.quote: mean accuracy r = 0.28, p,1025, one-sample t test, df = 14

entries.text: Single-trial spectrogram reconstruction was above zero in every participant (p<0.001 by individual randomization test).
entries.condition: Linear spectrogram model; single-trial cross-validated reconstruction; individual significance used 1,000 shuffled-trial reconstructions to form null distributions.
entries.quote: Across the sample of participants (N = 15), cross-validated reconstruction accuracy for single trials was significantly greater than zero in all individual participants (p,0.001, randomization test, Figure 3A).

entries.text: Mean linear reconstruction accuracy across acoustic frequency was reported in the approximate range r=0.2–0.3.
entries.condition: Population mean for the linear spectrogram model; frequency axis spans the analyzed spectrogram channels.

entries.text: The authors report significant predictive power largely in the high-gamma band.
entries.unit: Hz; p value; degrees of freedom
entries.condition: Across-participant prediction accuracy; one-sample tests against zero with Bonferroni correction. Methods separately state a 70–150 Hz extracted feature band (t8, t25).

entries.text: High-gamma predictive power exceeded that of other neural frequency bands (repeated-measures ANOVA F(30,420)=128.7, p<10^-10; adjusted pairwise p<0.05).
entries.condition: N=15 participants; 30 bands of 10 Hz from 1–300 Hz; pairwise comparisons Bonferroni adjusted.

entries.text: High-gamma extraction is specified as 70–150 Hz in Methods, while the Results and Figure 4 identify the high-gamma comparison as approximately 70–170 Hz.
entries.condition: Internal band-range discrepancy in the paper; the source does not reconcile it.
entries.loc: Materials and Methods, Participants and Neural Recordings; Results, Figure 4

entries.text: Reconstruction was lower with five or fewer responsive STG electrodes (mean r=0.19, N=6) and higher with 4-mm grids (mean r=0.43, N=4; mean 37 responsive STG electrodes per participant).
entries.unit: Pearson r; participants; responsive STG electrodes per participant
entries.condition: Groups are low responsive-electrode count (five or fewer) versus high-density-grid cases; overall prediction quality.
entries.quote: responsive STG electrodes (mean accuracy r=0.19, N =6

entries.text: Across participants, reconstruction accuracy correlated with frequency-spectrum coverage (r=0.78, p<0.001, df=13).
entries.unit: Pearson correlation; p value; degrees of freedom
entries.condition: Participant-level accuracy versus fraction of 180–7,000 Hz bins with one or more significant tuning peaks.

entries.text: Linear-model accuracy was significantly above zero for slow and intermediate modulation rates up to 8 Hz (r=0.15–0.42, p<0.0005; df=14), with Bonferroni correction.
entries.unit: Pearson r; Hz; p values; degrees of freedom
entries.condition: N=15; one-sample paired t tests; Bonferroni correction; linear spectrogram representation.

entries.text: Nonlinear modulation reconstruction outperformed the linear model overall (repeated-measures ANOVA F(1,14)=33.36, p<10^-4).
entries.condition: N=15; repeated-measures comparison of linear spectrogram and nonlinear modulation models; fast-rate comparison covers 4–32 Hz; Bonferroni-corrected post hoc tests.
entries.quote: In the group data, the nonlinear model yielded significantly higher accuracy compared to the linear model (two-way repeated measures ANOVA; main effect of model type, F(1,14) = 33.36, p,1024).

entries.text: Across 195 predictive STG sites, nonlinear rate tuning shifted to higher modulation rates than linear spectrogram tuning (paired t test p<10^-27, df=194); nonlinear sensitivity extended toward 32 Hz.
entries.unit: electrode sites; Hz; p value; degrees of freedom
entries.condition: Sites had forward prediction accuracy r>0.1; rate tuning estimated from linear and nonlinear STRF models.

entries.text: In rate-scale space, modulation-based reconstruction exceeded spectrogram-based reconstruction at temporal rates of at least 16 Hz for all spectral scales (p<0.05, corrected; interaction F(59,826)=1.84, p<0.0005).
entries.condition: N=15; post hoc pairwise tests Bonferroni corrected after two-way repeated-measures ANOVA.
entries.quote: modulation-based (nonlinear) decoding accuracy is significantly higher compared to frequency-based (linear) decoding (bottom) for all spectral scales at temporal rates $16 Hz

entries.text: The word-identification benchmark contained 47 isolated words and pseudowords from one speaker in one participant's 4-mm high-density-grid experiment.
entries.condition: The candidate vocabulary was closed-set; spectrogram reconstructions used single trials or averages of 3–5 trials per word.
entries.quote: Word identification based on the reconstructed spectrograms was assessed using a set of 47 individual words and pseudowords from a single speaker in a high density 4 mm grid experiment.

entries.text: Word scoring used dynamic time warping to align variable-duration words, then correlated each target reconstruction against candidate spectrograms; reported best performance used 2-D box smoothing of 500 ms by 2 octaves.
entries.unit: candidate words; smoothing duration; spectral smoothing width
entries.condition: Word identification was closed-set; no language-model decoding step is described (see t55).

entries.text: For averaged trials, median word-identification rank was 0.89 (p<0.0001 by randomization test).
entries.condition: One participant, 47-word/pseudoword set, single speaker, high-density 4-mm grid; averaged trials; the null median used 10,000 shuffled word-pairings.
entries.quote: Median identification rank is 0.89 (black arrow), which is higher than 0.50 chance level (dashed line; p,0.0001; randomization test).

entries.text: For single trials, median word-identification rank was 0.76 (p<0.0001 by randomization test).
entries.condition: Same one-speaker 47-candidate closed set and high-density-grid participant as t34; single-trial spectrogram reconstructions.
entries.quote: For single trials, identification performance declined slightly but remained significant (median = 0.76, p,0.0001; randomization test).

entries.text: The expected mean percentile rank under chance was 0.5.
entries.condition: Chance reference for the word-identification rank metric, not a classification accuracy or language-model baseline.
entries.quote:
The expected mean of the distribution of identifica-
tion ranks is 0.5 at chance level.

entries.text: Across word pairs, acoustic and reconstruction similarities correlated at r=0.41 (p<10^-10, df=45); this was computed before identification smoothing.
entries.unit: Pearson correlation; p value; degrees of freedom
entries.condition: Averaged-trial reconstructions; pairwise similarities between word spectrograms; before smoothing used in the identification algorithm.

entries.text: The authors concede that current reconstructions are not clearly intelligible to a human listener; the reported word readout used a rudimentary algorithm.
entries.condition: Applies to reconstructed acoustic output, including the supporting single-trial audio examples.
entries.quote: Single trial reconstructions are generally not intelligible.

entries.text: The authors note that low SNR or denser recordings might improve intelligibility, but the true STG features may not be invertible to an intelligible waveform and exact acoustic reconstruction may be impossible.
entries.condition: Interpretation of the gap between feature reconstruction and intelligible waveform reconstruction.

entries.text: Magnitude-only modulation reconstruction requires iterative phase retrieval; the authors warn that it causes non-neural errors and cannot perfectly recover even the original spectrogram.
entries.condition: Modulation-to-spectrogram projection was for visualization; quantitative model comparisons were performed in modulation space.

entries.text: Reported correlations were not corrected for the noise ceiling because sufficient repeated trials (more than 5) were generally unavailable for robust variability estimates.
entries.unit: repetitions generally unavailable for a robust estimate
entries.condition: All reported reconstruction correlations are uncorrected for potentially explainable variance due to trial-to-trial noise.
entries.quote: In the experiments reported here, a sufficient number of trial repetitions (.5) was generally unavailable for a robust estimate, and uncorrected values are therefore reported.

entries.text: The authors describe reconstruction as an upper bound on encoded features because their linear estimator does not model correlations among output variables.
entries.condition: Stimulus correlations and output-variable dependencies may affect reconstructed accuracy; the authors state different stimulus priors can examine stimulus-statistics effects.

entries.text: The authors state that exact physical-stimulus reconstruction is not expected because higher-order auditory processing can transform or discard acoustic information.
entries.condition: Reconstruction is used to characterize preserved features rather than assert that the entire input waveform is recoverable.

entries.text: The authors suggest the findings may support future readout of intended speech from brain activity; Discussion proposes neural interfaces and inner-speech readout as future work.
entries.condition: Future-facing possibility; no communication-interface or inner-speech experiment was conducted.

entries.text: The example audio was reconstructed from magnitude-only features with estimated phase; playback was slowed to 14 kHz although participants heard 16-kHz stimuli.
entries.condition: The paper warns that phase estimation introduces acoustic artifacts, so the audio is not a perfect reflection of the reconstructed representation.

entries.text: Random-subset resampling is reported, but random seeds for the split generation or model fitting are not stated.
entries.condition: Methods report 10 spectrogram and 3 modulation reconstruction resamples (and 20 forward-model resamples), without seed values.

entries.text: No speaker-disjoint or sentence-disjoint train/test split is specified; the detailed cross-validation partitions trials, so speaker overlap between train and test is not ruled out.
entries.condition: The paper separately says an out-of-sample word was evaluated in the Results; the relationship between that word-level description and the general trial-level split is not reconciled (see t49).

entries.text: The paper states that data were standardized, but does not say whether means and standard deviations were computed from training data only or included validation/test data.
entries.condition: This concerns the scope of normalization-statistic fitting, not whether z-scoring was performed; see t18 for the reported transformation.

entries.text: The Results describe leave-one-out evaluation of an out-of-sample word, while Methods describe random trial-level partitions; the paper does not map each headline aggregate to one protocol or clarify item-identity separation.
entries.condition: This ambiguity matters for whether repeated presentations or the same word identity could occur across train and test in each reported analysis.

entries.text: The paper reports the smoothing width that gave best word-identification performance but does not state how this width was selected or whether selection used validation or test data.
entries.condition: Selection-data provenance for the identification post-processing setting is not reported.
entries.quote: Best performance was achieved after smoothing the spectrograms with a 2-D box filter (500 ms, 2 octaves).

entries.text: Chance rank is defined for word identification (0.5), but the paper does not give a separate chance-level value for Pearson spectrogram/modulation reconstruction accuracy; those analyses test against zero or shuffled nulls.
entries.condition: Do not conflate the 0.5 rank baseline with a reconstruction-accuracy or open-vocabulary speech-recognition chance level.

entries.text: No language model or external lexical prior is described; the reported recognizer aligns words and ranks correlations against a fixed candidate set.
entries.condition: Closed-set 47-word/pseudoword task; do not treat this as open-vocabulary language-model decoding.

entries.text: No user confirmation stage or interactive confirmation outcome is described or evaluated.
entries.condition: The reported system is offline reconstruction and candidate-word ranking; no confirmation interaction is tested.

entries.text: No user correction mechanism, correction effort, or corrected-output evaluation is reported.
entries.condition: All reported reconstructions and word ranks are produced by the offline model and recognition procedure.

entries.text: No real-time use, online latency, long-term stability, or deployment evaluation is reported; the experiment is explicitly offline.
entries.condition: Clinical ECoG recordings were analyzed offline; neural communication interfaces are proposed only as a future possibility.

entries.text: The reported head-to-head evaluation is between the paper's linear spectrogram and nonlinear modulation representations; no external speech-reconstruction system benchmark is described.
entries.condition: Comparisons use this cohort and its cross-validation partitions, not a shared external benchmark.

entries.text: The authors interpret the results as supporting an emergent population-level representation of temporal modulation energy in primate auditory cortex and a possible dual coding scheme for slow and fast fluctuations.
entries.condition: Interpretive mechanism claim drawing on the human STG findings and cited nonhuman-primate work; the authors state that additional studies are needed.

entries.text: Linear-model accuracy was higher for slow rates ≤4 Hz than for faster rates >8 Hz (repeated-measures ANOVA F(5,70)=13.99, p<10^-8; corrected pairwise p<0.05).
entries.condition: N=15 participants; one-way repeated-measures ANOVA across modulation rates, followed by Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons.

entries.text: The nonlinear model improved accuracy at fast modulation rates; model-by-rate interaction F(5,70)=3.33, p<0.01, with post hoc p<10^-4.
entries.condition: N=15; two-way repeated-measures ANOVA comparing linear and nonlinear representations; post hoc pairwise tests Bonferroni corrected.
entries.quote: effect, F(5,70) = 3.33, p,0.01; post hoc pair-wise comparisons, p,1024, Bonferroni correction).

entries.condition: Visualization of modulation reconstruction projected to the spectrogram domain; quantitative comparisons were performed in modulation space.

entries.text: Dataset comprised seven patients undergoing neurosurgical procedures for epilepsy implanted with subdural electrode arrays.
entries.condition: dataset: 7 epilepsy patients; ECoG; overt speech condition

entries.text: The thesis's neural decoding is probabilistic: GMMs model firing-rate frames, and HMMs provide discrete-state sequence models with GMM emissions; HMMs are trained by Baum-Welch and decoded by Viterbi.
entries.condition: Chapter 4 frame classification and Chapter 5 discrete-state decoding; one subject, ER; no language model is reported.

entries.text: The thesis also summarizes earlier continuous-state vowel decoding with a Kalman filter that mapped neural activity to a two-dimensional formant-frequency trajectory; this is distinct from the thesis's GMM/HMM analyses.
entries.condition: Prior vowel-sequence study with subject ER and audio-visual feedback; performance was reported per trial block.

entries.text: The input representation is an ensemble of instantaneous neural firing-rate estimates from spike-sorted units, not an acoustic spectrogram or modulation-spectrum representation; 56 clusters were used in the Chapter 4 experiments.
entries.condition: Chapter 4; firing rates estimated at 10-ms spacing using binning, kernel smoothing, or adaptive exponential methods.

entries.text: Rate vectors were standardized per cluster before model fitting; GMM parameters were estimated by EM. Evaluation randomly partitioned trials into five folds, using four folds for training and one held-out fold for testing; no random seeds are stated.
entries.condition: Per recording date and one subject (ER); 4/5 trials train, 1/5 test; no speaker-independent split or seed information reported.

entries.text: For five-way frame classification (four vowels plus non-speech), 16-mixture GMMs with 100-ms binned-rate windows produced test error rates of 0.4154, 0.2962, and 0.3587 on the January, May, and October 2008 datasets, respectively; best test error was 0.2962.
entries.condition: Subject ER; May 19, 2008 recording; 10-ms frames, 100-ms bin window, 16-mixture GMM; five-fold trial-level cross-validation; vocabulary/classes are /aa/, /ae/, /ah/, /iy/, /uw/ plus silence/non-speech as described in the experiment (four vowels per recording date).

entries.text: For manually segmented VCV data from February 2, 2009, the best HMM segment-classification cross-validation accuracy was 0.524 (three states, eight mixtures); the best GMM result was 0.587.
entries.condition: One subject ER; 9 VCV trials / 63 segments; nine-fold cross-validation; known manual segment boundaries; no language model.

entries.text: Speech-activity detection was assessed with EER and minimum DCF, while vowel and phoneme tasks used frame/segment classification error or accuracy; no correlation-based reconstructed-waveform metric is reported.
entries.condition: Neural speech-activity detection; single subject ER; testing data were evaluated across recording dates and firing-rate/GMM configurations.

entries.text: This work evaluates neural classification and detection, not speech waveform reconstruction; it explicitly did not implement speech synthesis, so it provides no reconstruction-correlation result.
entries.condition: Chapter 5 discrete-state framework; one subject ER.

entries.text: Paper does not describe closed-set candidate scoring for auditory neural reconstruction; it uses Modified Rhyme Test (MRT) with 6-alternative forced choice for AV speech intelligibility.
